subtype: Approach: asking peers and seniors to critique it [Revision]
passage: Aditi, let old Nitin tell you about my first portfolio. I was so proud of it. Each project had a line: "Built with React, Node and MongoDB." Tools, tools, tools. A senior, Suresh Bhai, looked at it over tea and said, "Nitin, I know what you used. What happened because of it?" I had no answer. He said, "Tell me the problem, what you built, and what got better." I was quiet, then a little annoyed, and then I went home and rewrote everything. The hostel mess project became: "Students queued 20 minutes for tokens; I built a tap-to-order page; queue dropped to five." Suresh Bhai read it again and just nodded. That nod was worth ten compliments.

qa.q: What did Suresh Bhai ask about the tools?
qa.a: Suresh Bhai asked what happened because of them.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling right after the senior's question?
qa.a: Nitin was quiet and a little annoyed at first, because there was no answer to the question.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned the portfolio around, and why?
qa.a: Nitin rewrote each project around the problem, what was built and what got better, because outcomes showed value where a list of tools did not.

qa.q: How did Suresh Bhai see the first version of the portfolio?
qa.a: Suresh Bhai saw a long list of tools with no results, so he asked a plain question and nodded at the rewrite.

grounding: Shows getting critique from a senior, noticing that descriptions lack outcomes, and rewriting them around problem, work and result.

passage:
The application closed at midnight, the hostel wifi kept dropping, and Bhupen had just asked Uma, a senior now working at an analytics firm, to look at his portfolio over a crackly call.
'Your descriptions are all tools,' Uma said. 'Python, SQL, charts, cloud. I read three and I still don't know what any of it did.'
Bhupen scrolled. She was right. The canteen project said: 'Built using Python and SQL with interactive charts.'
'Then what do I write?'
'What was wrong before, what you made, what got better.'
The call dropped. Bhupen didn't wait for it to come back. By 10:30 the canteen project read: 'Lunch queues ran twenty minutes. I built a pre-order sheet for the canteen. Average wait fell to eight minutes over one month.' By 11:40 the other two were rewritten the same way. He submitted at 11:52, on his phone's hotspot.

qa.q: What did the canteen project description say before the rewrite?
qa.a: 'Built using Python and SQL with interactive charts.'

qa.q: What was Bhupen likely feeling when he scrolled and saw Uma was right?
qa.a: He likely felt a sting of embarrassment, then determination, since the deadline left no time to argue.

qa.q: What else could Bhupen do before the next application?
qa.a: Send the rewritten descriptions to Uma or another senior to check the results are clear, instead of rushing at night again.

qa.q: How does the old portfolio look to Uma?
qa.a: To Uma it is a list of tools that says nothing about what the work achieved, which is exactly what a recruiter would miss.

grounding: Shows a student taking a senior's critique that project write-ups list tools but not results, and rewriting each with the problem, the build and the improvement.

In the office canteen in Kochi, Asif, a senior developer who had once run a workshop at Elizabeth's college, opened her portfolio on his tablet between bites of appam.
'It's neat,' he said. 'But look at this line: "Tools used: JavaScript, maps, a database." That's a shopping list. What did the bus tracker actually do for anyone?'
Elizabeth thought for a second. 'Students at our college stopped missing the last bus. The warden said late passes dropped by half.'
'Then say that. Problem, what you built, what improved.'
That night, in her flat in Kakkanad, she rewrote all three projects. The bus tracker now began: 'Students kept missing the last college bus.' The tools moved to a small line at the end.
A week later Asif sent one word back: 'Better.' Two days after that, a recruiter asked her about the late passes.

qa.q: What did the tools line on Elizabeth's portfolio say?
How might Elizabeth have felt when Asif called her tools list a shopping list?
qa.a: She may have felt a little stung but curious, and she quickly found the real result, which suggests she took the comment as useful.

qa.q: What else could Elizabeth ask Asif to check next?
qa.a: Whether the results can be seen on a phone screen within a few seconds, since recruiters often skim.

qa.q: What changes for the recruiter after the rewrite?
qa.a: The recruiter now sees a real result, fewer missed buses and late passes, and has something concrete to ask about.

grounding: Shows a senior pointing out that project write-ups list tools but not outcomes, and the student rewriting each with problem, build and result.
